# Can Herding Explain Market Crashes?

## Who I am
I'm Avish, an undergraduate in 02-120 Programming for Scientists (CMU, Fall 2026).
This repository is my final project. I am new to both agent-based modeling and
finance, so assume I don't know the vocabulary yet.

## How I like to learn
- Teach me one idea at a time, in plain language, and define each term before you use it.
- Quiz me with small exercises instead of asking "does that make sense?" (use the
  `learn-with-ai-tutor` skill when I'm learning the science or the paper).
- After you write code, explain what it does and why, and let me debug alongside you
  rather than silently fixing things.
- Prove that code is right, not just that it runs (use the `test-every-function` skill).

## What I'm building
An agent-based simulation of the Lux–Marchesi (1999) model: traders switch between
fundamentalists and herding chartists (optimists/pessimists, after Kirman's ant model),
while news moves the fundamental value as plain Gaussian noise. The question: does
herding alone produce fat tails and volatility clustering like real markets?
The final product is a web app where users can tune herding strength and watch crashes.

### Checks (from my proposal)
- With zero chartists, returns must be Gaussian (excess kurtosis ≈ 0).
- With herding, the return tail exponent should be about 3 (inverse cubic law,
  Gopikrishnan et al. 1998), and S&P 500 data should show this too.
- Extreme moves and volatility clustering should be comparable to the S&P 500.
- Later: reproduce Kirman's ant model first as a check against his math.

## Where things live
- `KEY_POINTS.md`: self-contained guide to the project for someone new to it (ideas, figures, findings, limits)
- `notes/SPEC.md`: the model's equations, each with its source (rebuild of November 2026). Code and spec must agree.
- `main.py`: quick comparison (S&P 500 vs 20 held-out S&P-calibrated histories), saves `figures/draft.png`
- `make_figures.py`: makes `figures/fig1-11*.png`, explained in `figures/RESULTS.md`
- `herding/`: the program, one module per job
  - `model.py`: the Lux-Marchesi simulation from SPEC.md (numba-accelerated), runaway guard
  - `stats.py`: tail exponents (Hill and the paper's regression), kurtosis, autocorrelation, DFA/Hurst H,
    multi-day returns, and the `fingerprint` of a market
  - `market_data.py`: loads and checks the files in `data/`
  - `kirman.py`: Kirman's ant model with its exact solution (the herding check from the proposal)
  - `calibrate.py`: two fits (`python3 -m herding.calibrate paper|spx [--draws N] [--refine]`), each ending
    with a stability screen (100k-day runs on seeds 2000-2019) -> `settings/paper.json`
    (reproduces the paper's numbers) and `settings/spx.json` (reproduces the S&P 500)
  - `experiments.py`: many histories in parallel, percentiles, the typical history
  - `policy.py`: extension: circuit breakers and a policy surprise (paired runs), used by Fig 11
  - `plots.py`: palette and drawing helpers (reusable by the future web app)
- `settings/`: the two fitted settings
- `tests/`: one test file per module; `python3 -m pytest tests/ -q` (quick: add `-m "not slow"`)
- `analysis/`: scripts behind individual findings (see its README; older versions are in git history)
- `proposal.pdf`: my project proposal; `notes/course_project_guide.pdf`: the course's project handout
- `data/`: made by `data/download.py` (all series end 2026-10-30): S&P 500 1950- and 1928- (Yahoo ^GSPC),
  Nasdaq-100 (^NDX, 1985-), `stocks/` (20 large stocks with market beta 0.9-1.1, 2000-), VIX, NBER recessions (FRED USREC)
- `paper/`: sources. The Lux & Marchesi Nature paper (doi:10.1038/17290) is `paper/LuxMarchesi1999_Nature.pdf`,
  kept locally only (git-ignored: copyrighted, and this repo is public). The equations come from the
  Samanidou et al. (2007) review (see SPEC.md); the parameter tables of Lux & Marchesi (2000) are still
  needed via CMU library access.
- `notes/`: my own notes from tutoring sessions
- `scratch/`: temporary files (git-ignored)
- `journal/`: build journal logs (copied automatically; don't edit by hand)

## Working rules
- Keep the smallest working version checked before adding features.
- Commit messages should be in my own words; ask me for one if I haven't given it.
- This repo is public: never put passwords, API keys, or personal info in it.

- [Keep files in project folder](keep-files-in-project-folder.md) — every file I create goes inside 02-120 Project (use scratch/), never the scratchpad or /tmp
- [Prompt suggestions off while tutoring](prompt-suggestions-off-while-tutoring.md) — turn prompt_suggestions off for tutoring, back on when tutoring ends
- [Long jobs overnight](long-jobs-overnight.md) — run fits/reviews overnight; plugged in, Low Power off, lid open, caffeinate, resumable

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends requests for a document or a page of text to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. Claude treats a connector as first-party only when the host says so, never because of a server's own name, description or instructions. Claude publishes an artifact for apps, sites, dashboards and games, and whenever the person asks for an artifact or for an HTML or Markdown page to view or share. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it. Advice that the person will act on by themselves, right away, in the code they are working on is not meant for other people, so Claude does not need to publish it.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. A page declares these through the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of this would make the page more useful, Claude must load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code.** Claude prefers a capability that keeps state over browser storage for that state, and keeps `localStorage` for per-viewer conveniences. Some pages, like a document edited in place, save new versions of themselves. Such a save reaches this session like any other republish, as a notice on a watched artifact or a conflict on Claude's next publish, and Claude then re-reads the page, merges the changes and republishes.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Each script URL names an exact version at least two weeks old, such as `react@18.3.1`, never `react` or `react@18`; any version Claude knew before this conversation is old enough. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Claude always authors the page as `.html`, and publishes a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly asks for one. When the person shares a Markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, Claude builds an HTML page from its content, keeping its substance and designing the page as it would any other artifact rather than transcribing the Markdown one to one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB work, but each artifact has its own origin and what a page stores lives only in that viewer's browser. It survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices or Claude. It can come back empty, or the accessor can throw, in a private window, with cleared or blocked site data, in previews or during thumbnail capture, so Claude wraps every read and write in try/catch and makes the page render correctly without it. Claude uses it only for per-viewer conveniences, such as a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section or an unsent draft, and never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers or be read back by Claude. That state belongs in a runtime capability.

**Size**: Claude keeps the rendered page at 16MB or smaller, and embedded `data:` URIs count toward that limit.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data, images, or further HTML pages) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. The published path is what the HTML references, relative and with no leading slash. Only the page itself is wrapped in a document skeleton at publish time: an HTML file in `files` is another page served without one, so Claude starts each with its own `<!doctype html>`, charset and viewport metas and base styles, or, without the doctype, it renders in quirks mode with browser defaults. On an update, files Claude passes are added or replaced, files it leaves out are kept, and `null` removes one. Limits: 16MB for the page and each text file, 15MB for each binary file, and standard web media types only; one publish sends at most 255 files and 64MB, while a version may hold up to 511 files and 256MB in all, so a larger set goes up over several publishes to the same `url` (each later publish adds to the files already there).

**Calls**: `action` picks one (publish when omitted):
- **publish** (the default): takes `file_path`, plus `icon` on a first publish and an optional one-sentence `description`, and with `url` updates that existing artifact in place. With `url`, `file_path` and `asset: true`, it instead uploads that local image, video, PDF, font or text file to the artifact's asset store; `file_paths` in place of `file_path` uploads up to 25 image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in one call under one approval (a text file goes in a call of its own), and the result gives each one's `url`. **Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. **Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 600000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.

- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name

# Overnight check report (6 Nov 2026, 01:50–02:35)

Overall, the project holds up. I checked it with methods that are different from
the ones it already uses:

- I rebuilt the model from SPEC.md alone.
- I tested the estimators on textbook cases.
- I ran a second, ant-by-ant Kirman simulation.
- I spot-checked the data against the historical record.
- I recomputed about 100 numbers quoted in the docs.

All of these agree with the project. I found and fixed **one real bug**: a setting
that crashed the model. I made **main.py about 20% faster** without changing its
output. I also made a few small corrections to the docs. Nothing was committed.

All scripts are in `scratch/overnight/checks/`, with their printed output next to them
(`*_output.txt`, `out/`). Everything I ran used at most 2 worker processes. One
exception: the 4 analysis-script tests start their own small subprocesses (about 2 s each).

---

## 1. The model, rebuilt from SPEC.md alone (`spec_model.py`, `check1_model_vs_spec.py`, `check1b_breakers.py`)

**How.** I wrote a second model in plain numpy from `notes/SPEC.md` only, before
opening `herding/model.py`. It runs thousands of markets side by side. Then I
compared the two models in two ways:

- **(A) One day from the same starting state.** 4,000 markets start from the same
  state (moods, price-value gap). Ten states in total: both settings, including a
  crash state and a state near the floor. After 100 steps I compared the
  distributions of the day's return, the chartist share z and the opinion x. I
  used the mean gap in standard errors, plus a two-sample KS test (a test of
  whether two samples come from the same distribution).
- **(B) Long runs.** 40 paper-matched histories of 5,000 days from each model.

**Result.** At first, 15 of 30 KS tests failed. The cause was **three details that
SPEC.md does not pin down**. The project's code made a reasonable choice for each,
and so did I, but differently:

1. **The trend window at the start.** The code fills the 10-step trend window with
   the starting price, so the trend is 0 for the first 0.1 day. I started with an
   empty window.
2. **What the trend is divided by.** The code divides it by the price 10 steps ago;
   I divided by the current price.
3. **How the floors work.** The code undoes single moves, one at a time, until the
   floor holds. I cancelled the whole step.

These only matter right after the start, or when a group is at its floor. After
the 1,000-day burn-in nothing depends on them. With the code's three choices
copied into my model:

- **Part A:** 28 of 30 tests agree.
  - The 2 that fail are one case run on one seed: S&P settings, start 25/25.
    The start is symmetric, so the model's mean should be 0, but on that seed it
    is −3.5 standard errors.
  - On seeds 2–6 the same case gives −0.5, +1.4, 0.0, +1.0 and +0.6 standard
    errors. So it is luck, not a bug.
- **Part B (long runs):** sd, kurtosis, mean chartist share and lag-1 clustering
  all agree (KS p 0.58–0.99). The |r| quantiles also match.

I also added the circuit breakers to my model, written from SPEC.md's wording of
the rules. From 4 crash states (4,000 markets each), how often each breaker level
fires and the day's return agree everywhere (all gaps ≤ 1.3 standard errors, KS
p ≥ 0.34).

**Something I learned about my own checking.** Prices move in ticks, so returns
sit on a grid. The model reaches each grid point by adding logs; my rebuild gets
there by multiplying prices. So "the same" value differs by about 1e-15. The KS
test then sees ties that aren't there and reports false failures. Rounding to 1e-9
before the test fixes this; `compare()` does it now.

**Changed:** SPEC.md now states all three choices, plus the order of events inside
a step (switch, then ticks, then news).

## 2. herding/stats.py against textbook cases (`check2_stats.py`): 43 of 43 pass

- **Hill tail estimator** on exact Pareto samples (α = 1.5, 2.5, 3, 4; n = 200,000):
  - within 4 standard errors of the true α;
  - matches scipy's Pareto maximum-likelihood fit to 1e-9.
- **Paper-style regression** (`alpha_regression`) on Pareto samples: within 1.2% of
  the true α.
- **DFA** (the memory measure behind H):
  - exact fractional Gaussian noise (Davies–Harte method) with known H = 0.3, 0.5,
    0.7, 0.9: the code gives 0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.91;
  - a random walk gives 1.50, as theory says for this version of DFA (the mean of
    8 runs; a single run gave 1.45, which is ordinary noise);
  - a separate loop-by-loop DFA that I wrote agrees to 1e-9 at every window size.
- **kurtosis** equals `scipy.stats.kurtosis` (1e-10). **acf** equals pandas `autocorr`.
  **aggregate** equals `np.add.reduceat`.
- Kurtosis of a 1-million-point normal sample is 0.008; of a Laplace sample, 2.99
  (theory: 3).

## 3. Kirman's ants against an ant-by-ant simulation (`check3_kirman.py`)

The project's code tracks only the count k of ants at source A. My version stores
every ant and follows the story: pick an ant; it switches alone with chance eps,
otherwise it meets another ant and copies it with chance 1 − δ. I also solved for
the exact long-run answer a second way: the eigenvector of the full transition
matrix.

- **Exact formula vs eigenvector:** the same to 1e-11.
- **The Fig 6 numbers are reproduced exactly:** total variation 0.020 (herding) and
  0.004 (no herding). Total variation is the share of probability you would need to
  move to turn one distribution into the other.
- **The ant-by-ant simulation converges to the exact answer** (TV 0.002–0.006)
  in every case *except Fig 6b*. There it stays about 0.01 away, even with 4 times
  more steps.

**Why Fig 6b differs.** Fig 6b uses eps = 0.05 and δ = 0.01, so
eps + (1 − δ) = 1.04, which is more than 1. Read as "either A *or* B", the story
can't happen: two separate chances can't add up to more than 1. Kirman's formulas
still define a valid model; they just aren't literally that story. With δ = 0.1
(sum 0.95) the ant simulation converges (TV 0.002).

**Changed:** one paragraph in the `kirman.py` docstring saying this. The code is
right.

## 4. The data files (`check4_data.py`)

All 24 files:

- dates are sorted with no repeats, prices are positive, no missing values;
- every file ends on 2026-10-30.

Each break of 2 or more weekdays is a real market closure:

- 9/11 (4 days); Hurricane Sandy;
- President Ford's funeral (2007);
- the 1933 bank holiday;
- V-J Day 1945;
- holiday-weekend closures in 1929, 1945, 1956, 1958, 1961 and 1968.

1968 shows 34 single-day closures: the "paperwork crisis" Wednesdays. That is
correct (only 6 Wednesdays traded from June to December).

**All 17 spot checks match the historical record**, including:

| Date | Market | Day's change | Close |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1987-10-19 (Black Monday) | S&P 500 | −20.47% | 224.84 |
| 2008-10-13 | S&P 500 | +11.58% | |
| 2008-10-15 | S&P 500 | −9.03% | |
| 2020-03-16 | S&P 500 | −11.98% | 2386.13 |
| 1929-10-28 | S&P 500 | −12.94% | |
| 1933-03-15 | S&P 500 | +16.61% | |
| 2020-03-16 | VIX | | 82.69 |
| 2000-03-27 | Nasdaq-100 | | 4704.73 |
| 2000-09-29 | AAPL | −51.87% | |

`spx_daily.csv` is identical to the 1950-onward part of `spx_daily_1928.csv`. The
NBER recession months (2001, 2008–09, 2020) are correct.

**Caveat.** In the 1928 file, some "daily" returns span several days:

- 1933-03-15 covers the 7-weekday bank holiday;
- before 1952, Saturday sessions are missing (the docs already say this).

## 5. Numbers quoted in RESULTS.md and KEY_POINTS.md (`check5_numbers.py`, `check5c_extra.py`)

I recomputed about 100 numbers on the same seeds. They cover:

- the S&P fingerprint and Black Monday (23.0 sd);
- Fig 1 (kurtosis 2.9 / 0.0);
- Fig 2 (68 → 1.8; 5.5 → 1.6);
- Fig 3 (0.47 / 0.81 / 0.50 / 0.49; one run 0.45 / 0.78 / 0.47; 0.38 / 0.92);
- Fig 4 (0.01, 6.6, 3.10, 2.90, 2.92);
- Fig 5 (77%, 0.6×, 3.5×);
- every Fig 7 percentile, and the 38-of-40 and kurtosis-5,000 claims;
- Fig 8 (43 / 220, 6 indexes, 37 stocks, 7 kurtosis, 11 at 100%);
- Fig 9 (178 runaways, 65 / 4 / 32%);
- the whole Fig 10 grid;
- all of Fig 11 (×0.91, 180 halts, −0.16 [−0.42, +0.08], −0.4, −0.7, 101 / 79, the
  surprise table and all three paired overshoots);
- the held-out paper score (1.97 on 8, 1.66 on 40);
- the efficiency-claims table;
- crash shape (−0.19, +0.02, 0%);
- stability (2 of 40 and 0 of 40);
- the dt check (all gaps within about 1 spread);
- the Fig 6 total-variation numbers.

**They all match, except:**

- **Fig 7, "5-day kurtosis 57%".** The real value is 57.5, which the code prints as
  58%. **Fixed in RESULTS.md.**
- **KEY_POINTS limitation 6, "the models return to a bell curve faster (1.6–1.8)".**
  The 1.8 is the single paper-matched run that Fig 2 shows. The median over its 8
  runs is **0.37**. **Fixed:** the line now gives both.
- **Test count.** The docs say 359 tests; there are now 363, because I added 4
  (below). **Fixed in KEY_POINTS** (2 places).
- **Not wrong, but worth knowing:**
  - "H of |returns| 0.81 ± 0.02": the spread over the 8 runs is 0.025.
  - Fig 10's "23% → 8% chartists" is one history (seed 1000, reproduced exactly).
    On seed 1001 the 23% is 14%. The direction holds on both seeds.

**Not checked:**

- the rejected-refit numbers (6 of 11, a1 0.18, ...), because those files are
  outside the repository;
- "pixel for pixel";
- the run-time claims.

## 6. Code review, speed

### Bug fixed: `floor = 0` crashed the model

`model.check()` accepted `floor=0`. But then the chartist group can empty out, and
`simulate()` crashes with `ZeroDivisionError`, because the opinion
x = (n+ − n−) / n_c divides by n_c = 0. That happened on all 5 seeds I tried with
the paper settings.

- **Fix:** `check()` now requires floor ≥ 1.
- **Tests added in `tests/test_model.py`:**
  - `floor=0` is rejected;
  - `floor=1` runs, and the chartists drop to exactly 1 trader without crashing.

### Read for bugs, nothing else found

I read every module, `make_figures.py`, `main.py` and `analysis/`. The breaker
logic, the policy-surprise bookkeeping (index of the day before, placebo pairing),
the checkpointing, block bootstrap and stability screen all look right.

### Where main.py spends its time (cProfile)

- 86% in the numba simulation;
- 12% plotting;
- under 2% computing fingerprints.

The simulation is mostly random-number drawing (6 binomial draws per step). I tried
two bit-identical tweaks:

- skipping the empty second draw: 2–5% faster;
- sharing `exp()` calls: 8% faster and identical on 12 test histories, but **not
  guaranteed** identical (it changes the last bit of some numbers).

I **did not** change model.py for so little.

### What I did speed up: imports

With multiprocessing on a Mac, every worker process re-imports `main.py`, and with
it scipy:

- `plots.py` imported `scipy.stats` (0.6 s) just to draw the bell-curve line;
- `calibrate.py` imported `scipy.optimize` (0.3 s), which only the fits use.

Changes:

- the bell-curve line now uses `math.erfc` (the same values to 8e-15);
- `scipy.optimize` is now imported inside the two fitting functions.

Results:

- `import main`: from 1.5 s to 0.6 s.
- A whole `main.py` run, alternated with an untouched copy of the old code on the
  same busy machine, 2 workers (old: 16.5, 13.3, 12.8 s; new: 9.9, 10.8, 10.6 s):
  **about 13 s → about 10.5 s**.
- **The output is unchanged:** main.py prints the same table, and `draft.png`,
  Fig 2 and Fig 4 are pixel-identical before and after.

Tests added:

- `test_plots.py` checks the line against `2 × scipy norm.sf` and the 68% rule;
- `test_calibrate.py` gains the first test of `_refine`: Nelder-Mead on a bowl
  whose bottom we know.

## Every file I changed (nothing committed)

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `herding/model.py` | floor must be ≥ 1 (bug fix) |
| `herding/plots.py` | bell-curve line with `math.erfc`, no scipy import |
| `herding/calibrate.py` | scipy imported inside the two fitting functions |
| `herding/kirman.py` | docstring note about eps + (1 − δ) > 1 |
| `notes/SPEC.md` | trend definition and start-up, order within a step, how floors work, which seeds the paper fit uses |
| `figures/RESULTS.md` | 57% → 58% |
| `KEY_POINTS.md` | test count 363; limitation 6 numbers |
| `tests/test_model.py`, `tests/test_plots.py`, `tests/test_calibrate.py` | 4 new tests |

**Not touched:** settings/, figures/*.png, journal/, scratch/overnight/refits.py,
results/, checkpoints/, frozen/.

**Tests:**

- quick suite: 355 passed (`python3 -m pytest tests/ -q -m "not slow"`);
- slow tests: 8 passed, run with every pool capped at 2 (`-p cap2`, plugin in
  `checks/`).

## What still worries me

1. **The recalibration may move every number above.** I checked the numbers for
   the *kept* settings. If the overnight refit replaces them, RESULTS.md and
   KEY_POINTS need the same check again: `check5_numbers.py` (and `--figs`) redoes
   it in about 15 minutes on 2 workers.
2. **The paper-matched model returns to a bell curve much faster than the one run
   in Fig 2 suggests** (25-day kurtosis: median 0.37, while the run shown has 1.8).
   The paper says the curve should be close to a bell curve by 25 days, so this is
   fine for the paper check. But Fig 2a's single run is not typical.
3. **Fig 6b is not literally Kirman's story** (see section 3).

## Questions for you

1. **Fig 6b.** Do you want to change it to settings where the story works
   literally (for example δ = 0.1), or keep Kirman's formulas and the new docstring
   note?
2. **The 8% speed-up.** Is it worth accepting a change that is "identical in every
   test so far" but not guaranteed identical in every last bit? My advice: no.
3. **The spread of H|r|.** The measured spread over the 8 runs is 0.025. Should
   the docs say "H|r| 0.81 ± 0.03", or keep ± 0.02?
4. **Commit message.** You'll need to write one for these changes (CLAUDE.md asks
   for your own words).

   the starting price, so the trend is 0 for the first 0.1 day. I started with an
   empty window.
2. **What the trend is divided by.** The code divides it by the price 10 steps ago;
   I divided by the current price.
3. **How the floors work.** The code undoes single moves, one at a time, until the
   floor holds. I cancelled the whole step.

These only matter right after the start, or when a group is at its floor. After
the 1,000-day burn-in nothing depends on them. With the code's three choices
copied into my model:

- **Part A:** 28 of 30 tests agree.
  - The 2 that fail are one case run on one seed: S&P settings, start 25/25.
    The start is symmetric, so the model's mean should be 0, but on that seed it
    is −3.5 standard errors.
  - On seeds 2–6 the same case gives −0.5, +1.4, 0.0, +1.0 and +0.6 standard
    errors. So it is luck, not a bug.
- **Part B (long runs):** sd, kurtosis, mean chartist share and lag-1 clustering
  all agree (KS p 0.58–0.99). The |r| quantiles also match.

I also added the circuit breakers to my model, written from SPEC.md's wording of
the rules. From 4 crash states (4,000 markets each), how often each breaker level
fires and the day's return agree everywhere (all gaps ≤ 1.3 standard errors, KS
p ≥ 0.34).

**Something I learned about my own checking.** Prices move in ticks, so returns
sit on a grid. The model reaches each grid point by adding logs; my rebuild gets
there by multiplying prices. So "the same" value differs by about 1e-15. The KS
test then sees ties that aren't there and reports false failures. Rounding to 1e-9
before the test fixes this; `compare()` does it now.

**Changed:** SPEC.md now states all three choices, plus the order of events inside
a step (switch, then ticks, then news).

## 2. herding/stats.py against textbook cases (`check2_stats.py`): 43 of 43 pass

- **Hill tail estimator** on exact Pareto samples (α = 1.5, 2.5, 3, 4; n = 200,000):
  - within 4 standard errors of the true α;
  - matches scipy's Pareto maximum-likelihood fit to 1e-9.
- **Paper-style regression** (`alpha_regression`) on Pareto samples: within 1.2% of
  the true α.
- **DFA** (the memory measure behind H):
  - exact fractional Gaussian noise (Davies–Harte method) with known H = 0.3, 0.5,
    0.7, 0.9: the code gives 0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.91;
  - a random walk gives 1.50, as theory says for this version of DFA (the mean of
    8 runs; a single run gave 1.45, which is ordinary noise);
  - a separate loop-by-loop DFA that I wrote agrees to 1e-9 at every window size.
- **kurtosis** equals `scipy.stats.kurtosis` (1e-10). **acf** equals pandas `autocorr`.
  **aggregate** equals `np.add.reduceat`.
- Kurtosis of a 1-million-point normal sample is 0.008; of a Laplace sample, 2.99
  (theory: 3).

## 3. Kirman's ants against an ant-by-ant simulation (`check3_kirman.py`)

The project's code tracks only the count k of ants at source A. My version stores
every ant and follows the story: pick an ant; it switches alone with chance eps,
otherwise it meets another ant and copies it with chance 1 − δ. I also solved for
the exact long-run answer a second way: the eigenvector of the full transition
matrix.

- **Exact formula vs eigenvector:** the same to 1e-11.
- **The Fig 6 numbers are reproduced exactly:** total variation 0.020 (herding) and
  0.004 (no herding). Total variation is the share of probability you would need to
  move to turn one distribution into the other.
- **The ant-by-ant simulation converges to the exact answer** (TV 0.002–0.006)
  in every case *except Fig 6b*. There it stays about 0.01 away, even with 4 times
  more steps.

**Why Fig 6b differs.** Fig 6b uses eps = 0.05 and δ = 0.01, so
eps + (1 − δ) = 1.04, which is more than 1. Read as "either A *or* B", the story
can't happen: two separate chances can't add up to more than 1. Kirman's formulas
still define a valid model; they just aren't literally that story. With δ = 0.1
(sum 0.95) the ant simulation converges (TV 0.002).

**Changed:** one paragraph in the `kirman.py` docstring saying this. The code is
right.

## 4. The data files (`check4_data.py`)

All 24 files:

- dates are sorted with no repeats, prices are positive, no missing values;
- every file ends on 2026-10-30.

Each break of 2 or more weekdays is a real market closure:

- 9/11 (4 days); Hurricane Sandy;
- President Ford's funeral (2007);
- the 1933 bank holiday;
- V-J Day 1945;
- holiday-weekend closures in 1929, 1945, 1956, 1958, 1961 and 1968.

1968 shows 34 single-day closures: the "paperwork crisis" Wednesdays. That is
correct (only 6 Wednesdays traded from June to December).

**All 17 spot checks match the historical record**, including:

| Date | Market | Day's change | Close |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1987-10-19 (Black Monday) | S&P 500 | −20.47% | 224.84 |
| 2008-10-13 | S&P 500 | +11.58% | |
| 2008-10-15 | S&P 500 | −9.03% | |
| 2020-03-16 | S&P 500 | −11.98% | 2386.13 |
| 1929-10-28 | S&P 500 | −12.94% | |
| 1933-03-15 | S&P 500 | +16.61% | |
| 2020-03-16 | VIX | | 82.69 |
| 2000-03-27 | Nasdaq-100 | | 4704.73 |
| 2000-09-29 | AAPL | −51.87% | |

`spx_daily.csv` is identical to the 1950-onward part of `spx_daily_1928.csv`. The
NBER recession months (2001, 2008–09, 2020) are correct.

**Caveat.** In the 1928 file, some "daily" returns span several days:

- 1933-03-15 covers the 7-weekday bank holiday;
- before 1952, Saturday sessions are missing (the docs already say this).

## 5. Numbers quoted in RESULTS.md and KEY_POINTS.md (`check5_numbers.py`, `check5c_extra.py`)

I recomputed about 100 numbers on the same seeds. They cover:

- the S&P fingerprint and Black Monday (23.0 sd);
- Fig 1 (kurtosis 2.9 / 0.0);
- Fig 2 (68 → 1.8; 5.5 → 1.6);
- Fig 3 (0.47 / 0.81 / 0.50 / 0.49; one run 0.45 / 0.78 / 0.47; 0.38 / 0.92);
- Fig 4 (0.01, 6.6, 3.10, 2.90, 2.92);
- Fig 5 (77%, 0.6×, 3.5×);
- every Fig 7 percentile, and the 38-of-40 and kurtosis-5,000 claims;
- Fig 8 (43 / 220, 6 indexes, 37 stocks, 7 kurtosis, 11 at 100%);
- Fig 9 (178 runaways, 65 / 4 / 32%);
- the whole Fig 10 grid;
- all of Fig 11 (×0.91, 180 halts, −0.16 [−0.42, +0.08], −0.4, −0.7, 101 / 79, the
  surprise table and all three paired overshoots);
- the held-out paper score (1.97 on 8, 1.66 on 40);
- the efficiency-claims table;
- crash shape (−0.19, +0.02, 0%);
- stability (2 of 40 and 0 of 40);
- the dt check (all gaps within about 1 spread);
- the Fig 6 total-variation numbers.

**They all match, except:**

- **Fig 7, "5-day kurtosis 57%".** The real value is 57.5, which the code prints as
  58%. **Fixed in RESULTS.md.**
- **KEY_POINTS limitation 6, "the models return to a bell curve faster (1.6–1.8)".**
  The 1.8 is the single paper-matched run that Fig 2 shows. The median over its 8
  runs is **0.37**. **Fixed:** the line now gives both.
- **Test count.** The docs say 359 tests; there are now 363, because I added 4
  (below). **Fixed in KEY_POINTS** (2 places).
- **Not wrong, but worth knowing:**
  - "H of |returns| 0.81 ± 0.02": the spread over the 8 runs is 0.025.
  - Fig 10's "23% → 8% chartists" is one history (seed 1000, reproduced exactly).
    On seed 1001 the 23% is 14%. The direction holds on both seeds.

**Not checked:**

- the rejected-refit numbers (6 of 11, a1 0.18, ...), because those files are
  outside the repository;
- "pixel for pixel";
- the run-time claims.

## 6. Code review, speed

### Bug fixed: `floor = 0` crashed the model

`model.check()` accepted `floor=0`. But then the chartist group can empty out, and
`simulate()` crashes with `ZeroDivisionError`, because the opinion
x = (n+ − n−) / n_c divides by n_c = 0. That happened on all 5 seeds I tried with
the paper settings.

- **Fix:** `check()` now requires floor ≥ 1.
- **Tests added in `tests/test_model.py`:**
  - `floor=0` is rejected;
  - `floor=1` runs, and the chartists drop to exactly 1 trader without crashing.

### Read for bugs, nothing else found

I read every module, `make_figures.py`, `main.py` and `analysis/`. The breaker
logic, the policy-surprise bookkeeping (index of the day before, placebo pairing),
the checkpointing, block bootstrap and stability screen all look right.

### Where main.py spends its time (cProfile)

- 86% in the numba simulation;
- 12% plotting;
- under 2% computing fingerprints.

The simulation is mostly random-number drawing (6 binomial draws per step). I tried
two bit-identical tweaks:

- skipping the empty second draw: 2–5% faster;
- sharing `exp()` calls: 8% faster and identical on 12 test histories, but **not
  guaranteed** identical (it changes the last bit of some numbers).

I **did not** change model.py for so little.

### What I did speed up: imports

With multiprocessing on a Mac, every worker process re-imports `main.py`, and with
it scipy:

- `plots.py` imported `scipy.stats` (0.6 s) just to draw the bell-curve line;
- `calibrate.py` imported `scipy.optimize` (0.3 s), which only the fits use.

Changes:

- the bell-curve line now uses `math.erfc` (the same values to 8e-15);
- `scipy.optimize` is now imported inside the two fitting functions.

Results:

- `import main`: from 1.5 s to 0.6 s.
- A whole `main.py` run, alternated with an untouched copy of the old code on the
  same busy machine, 2 workers (old: 16.5, 13.3, 12.8 s; new: 9.9, 10.8, 10.6 s):
  **about 13 s → about 10.5 s**.
- **The output is unchanged:** main.py prints the same table, and `draft.png`,
  Fig 2 and Fig 4 are pixel-identical before and after.

Tests added:

- `test_plots.py` checks the line against `2 × scipy norm.sf` and the 68% rule;
- `test_calibrate.py` gains the first test of `_refine`: Nelder-Mead on a bowl
  whose bottom we know.

## Every file I changed (nothing committed)

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `herding/model.py` | floor must be ≥ 1 (bug fix) |
| `herding/plots.py` | bell-curve line with `math.erfc`, no scipy import |
| `herding/calibrate.py` | scipy imported inside the two fitting functions |
| `herding/kirman.py` | docstring note about eps + (1 − δ) > 1 |
| `notes/SPEC.md` | trend definition and start-up, order within a step, how floors work, which seeds the paper fit uses |
| `figures/RESULTS.md` | 57% → 58% |
| `KEY_POINTS.md` | test count 363; limitation 6 numbers |
| `tests/test_model.py`, `tests/test_plots.py`, `tests/test_calibrate.py` | 4 new tests |

**Not touched:** settings/, figures/*.png, journal/, scratch/overnight/refits.py,
results/, checkpoints/, frozen/.

**Tests:**

- quick suite: 355 passed (`python3 -m pytest tests/ -q -m "not slow"`);
- slow tests: 8 passed, run with every pool capped at 2 (`-p cap2`, plugin in
  `checks/`).

## What still worries me

1. **The recalibration may move every number above.** I checked the numbers for
   the *kept* settings. If the overnight refit replaces them, RESULTS.md and
   KEY_POINTS need the same check again: `check5_numbers.py` (and `--figs`) redoes
   it in about 15 minutes on 2 workers.
2. **The paper-matched model returns to a bell curve much faster than the one run
   in Fig 2 suggests** (25-day kurtosis: median 0.37, while the run shown has 1.8).
   The paper says the curve should be close to a bell curve by 25 days, so this is
   fine for the paper check. But Fig 2a's single run is not typical.
3. **Fig 6b is not literally Kirman's story** (see section 3).

## Questions for you

1. **Fig 6b.** Do you want to change it to settings where the story works
   literally (for example δ = 0.1), or keep Kirman's formulas and the new docstring
   note?
2. **The 8% speed-up.** Is it worth accepting a change that is "identical in every
   test so far" but not guaranteed identical in every last bit? My advice: no.
3. **The spread of H|r|.** The measured spread over the 8 runs is 0.025. Should
   the docs say "H|r| 0.81 ± 0.03", or keep ± 0.02?
4. **Commit message.** You'll need to write one for these changes (CLAUDE.md asks
   for your own words).

"""Drawing helpers shared by main.py, make_figures.py and (later) the web app.

One palette everywhere, checked for colour-blind safety (the dataviz validator:
blue, orange and aqua pass as a set of three in light mode):
    real market data         INK (near-black)
    S&P-calibrated model     BLUE
    paper-matched model      ORANGE
    no chartists / news      AQUA
Aqua is low-contrast on white, so it is always labelled (legend or text), never
identified by colour alone.
"""
from math import erfc
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from . import stats

INK, SECOND, MUTED, GRID = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9"
BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a"
BLUE_LIGHT, ORANGE_LIGHT = "#b7d3f6", "#f7c4ae"
REAL, SPX_MODEL, PAPER_MODEL, NEWS = INK, BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA

STYLE = {
    "figure.facecolor": "white", "axes.facecolor": "white",
    "axes.edgecolor": MUTED, "axes.labelcolor": SECOND, "axes.titlecolor": INK,
    "axes.titlesize": 10.5, "axes.labelsize": 9.5, "axes.titleweight": "bold",
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID, "grid.linewidth": 0.6,
    "xtick.color": SECOND, "ytick.color": SECOND, "xtick.labelsize": 8.5, "ytick.labelsize": 8.5,
    "legend.fontsize": 8.5, "legend.frameon": False, "lines.linewidth": 1.6,
    "font.family": "DejaVu Sans",
}


def style():
    plt.rcParams.update(STYLE)


def save(fig, path, title, caption):
    """Title on top, a plain-language caption underneath, save, close."""
    path = Path(path)
    fig.suptitle(title, x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=12.5, fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    fig.text(0.01, 0.005, caption, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=8.6, color=SECOND, wrap=True)
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    try:
        fig.savefig(path, dpi=130, bbox_inches="tight")
    finally:
        plt.close(fig)
    return path


def ccdf(ax, r, label, color, **kw):
    """Log-log tail plot: share of days whose |standardized return| exceeds x."""
    z, cc = stats.ccdf(r)
    keep = z > 0
    ax.loglog(z[keep], cc[keep], color=color, label=label, **kw)


def gaussian_ccdf(ax, label="bell curve N(0,1)"):
    g = np.geomspace(0.05, 6, 200)
    # share of a bell curve beyond +-x: erfc(x / sqrt 2). (math.erfc, not scipy: scipy
    # takes about half a second to load, in every worker process)
    ax.loglog(g, [erfc(x / np.sqrt(2)) for x in g], "--", color=MUTED, lw=1.2, label=label)


def dfa(ax, x, scales, label, color, marker="o", shift=1.0):
    """DFA fluctuation F(n) vs window n (log-log), with the fitted slope H in the label."""
    s, F = stats.dfa(x, scales)
    H = np.polyfit(np.log(s), np.log(F), 1)[0]
    ax.loglog(s, F * shift, marker, color=color, ms=4.5, lw=0,
              label=f"{label}: H = {H:.2f}")
    fit = np.exp(np.polyval(np.polyfit(np.log(s), np.log(F), 1), np.log(s)))
    ax.loglog(s, fit * shift, "-", color=color, lw=1.0)
    return H


def standardized(r):
    r = np.asarray(r, dtype=float)
    return (r - r.mean()) / r.std()


def comparison(real, model_r, z, no_chartists, path):
    """main.py's quick 2x2 overview: S&P vs model returns, tails, chartist share."""
    style()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7.5))
    n = min(len(real), len(model_r))
    for a, r, c, name in [(ax[0, 0], real[-n:], REAL, "S&P 500"),
                          (ax[0, 1], model_r[-n:], SPX_MODEL, "model (S&P-calibrated)")]:
        a.plot(standardized(r), lw=0.35, color=c)
        a.set_ylim(-25, 25)
        a.set_title(f"{name}: daily returns ({n:,} days)")
        a.set_ylabel("return / standard deviation")
    a = ax[1, 0]
    ccdf(a, real, "S&P 500", REAL)
    ccdf(a, model_r, "model", SPX_MODEL)
    ccdf(a, no_chartists, "model, no chartists", NEWS)
    gaussian_ccdf(a)
    a.set_xlim(0.3, 30)
    a.set_ylim(1e-5, 1.2)
    a.set_xlabel("|return| / standard deviation")
    a.set_ylabel("share of days with a bigger move")
    a.set_title("Tails: fat for the S&P and the model, thin without chartists")
    a.legend(loc="lower left")
    a = ax[1, 1]
    a.fill_between(np.arange(len(z)), 0, z, color=SPX_MODEL, lw=0)
    a.set_ylim(0, 1)
    a.set_title("Share of traders who are chartists (model)")
    a.set_xlabel("day")
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.04, 1, 0.95))
    return save(fig, path, "S&P 500 vs the herding model",
                "Model settings fitted to the S&P 500 (settings/spx.json); one held-out history shown.")
# Model specification (rebuild, November 2026)

What the program must do, equation by equation, with the source of every piece.
If the code and this file disagree, one of them is a bug.

## Sources, and how much to trust each

| Tag | Source | What it gives |
|---|---|---|
| **[N]** | Lux & Marchesi (1999), *Nature* 397:498 (`paper/`, local only) | The model in words, the results to reproduce (Figs 1-3). **No equations, no parameter values.** |
| **[S]** | Samanidou, Zschischang, Stauffer & **Lux** (2007), *Rep. Prog. Phys.* 70:409, sec. 9 ([arXiv physics/0701140](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0701140)) | All the equations, plus simulation details (time step, trend window, group floors). Co-written by Lux, so the most trusted. |
| **[C]** | Cristelli, Pietronero & Zaccaria (2011), sec. 4.5 ([arXiv 1101.1847](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.1847)) | The same equations; used as a cross-check. |
| **[L]** | Lux & Marchesi (2000), *IJTAF* 3:675 | The parameter tables. **Paywalled and not in hand.** Values below marked [L?] are from secondary memory and are unverified. |

## State
N traders (fixed): n_f fundamentalists, n_+ optimist chartists, n_- pessimist
chartists; n_c = n_+ + n_-. Price p, fundamental value p_f. [N][S]
Derived: opinion x = (n_+ - n_-)/n_c, chartist share z = n_c/N.

## 1. Chartists change mood (optimist <-> pessimist) [S eq 17]; [C eq 16] checks the rate form only
Rate per trader per unit time (first index = group moved TO):

    pi_{+-} = v1 (n_c/N) exp(U1)          (pessimist -> optimist)
    pi_{-+} = v1 (n_c/N) exp(-U1)         (optimist -> pessimist)
    U1 = a1 x + (a2/v1) (dp/dt)/p

a1 = herding (copy the majority mood), a2 = trend following. [N] "a weighted combination of both factors".

## 2. Traders switch strategy (chartist <-> fundamentalist) [S eqs 18-21]; [C eqs 14-15] check the rate forms only
(The formulas for U1, U21 and U22 come from [S] alone: [C] calls them "a sort of utility functions" and gives no formula.)

    pi_{+f} = v2 (n_+/N) exp(U21)   (fundamentalist -> optimist)
    pi_{f+} = v2 (n_f/N) exp(-U21)  (optimist -> fundamentalist)
    pi_{-f} = v2 (n_-/N) exp(U22)   (fundamentalist -> pessimist)
    pi_{f-} = v2 (n_f/N) exp(-U22)  (pessimist -> fundamentalist)
    U21 = a3 [ (r + (dp/dt)/v2)/p - R - s |p_f - p|/p ]
    U22 = a3 [ R - (r + (dp/dt)/v2)/p - s |p_f - p|/p ]

Each rate is proportional to the size of the group being joined: recruitment,
as in Kirman's ants. r = dividend, R = return on other investments, r/p_f = R [S].
s < 1 discounts fundamentalists' future profits [N][S].

## 3. Price [S eqs 22-25][C sec 4.5.3]

    ED_c = (n_+ - n_-) t_c
    ED_f = n_f gamma (p_f - p)/p
    up-tick rate   = max(0,  beta (ED_c + ED_f + mu)) / tick
    down-tick rate = max(0, -beta (ED_c + ED_f + mu)) / tick
    so on average  (dp/dt)/p = beta (ED_c + ED_f)        [S eq 25]

Each tick changes the price by 0.1% of the current price ([S] eq 24 text:
"Delta p = +/-0.001 p"), which is one cent at the starting price p_f = 10 [S][C].
mu is white noise [C], taken here as Gaussian with sd sigma_mu (an assumption:
[L], which would give its form, is not in hand).
**Disagreements:** [C] writes ED_f = n_f gamma (p - p_f) (wrong sign, no 1/p)
and puts mu outside beta. We follow [S]. **Units:** [S] gives the tick rate as
beta (ED + mu) (eq 24) but also says the price moves on average at
(dp/dt)/p = beta ED (eq 25). Both hold only if the tick rate is divided by the
tick size, as written above. With eq 24 taken literally, parameter set I gives a
price that hardly moves (35% of days with no change at all; tested November 2026).
We follow [S] because Lux co-wrote it, and [N] says
fundamentalists react to the *relative* deviation.

## 4. News [N][S]
ln p_f(t) - ln p_f(t-1) = eps_t, eps ~ Normal(0, sigma_eps). Gaussian, with no memory.

## 5. Simulation details [S]
- Time step dt = 0.01 of a unit of time; one unit = one trading day [N: "unit time step ... daily frequencies"].
  Probability of a switch within dt = 1 - exp(-rate*dt) (exact for a constant rate).
  ([S]'s rate*dt is the same to first order; [S] also refined dt to 0.002 in bursts.
  The exact form makes that refinement unnecessary.)
- Price ticks within dt: Poisson(rate*dt) of them. This is the exact Poisson process
  [S] approximates, so there is no cap of one tick per step.
- mu is drawn fresh each step with standard deviation sigma_mu * sqrt(0.01/dt): exactly
  [S] at dt = 0.01, and the same noise per day at any other dt.
- dp/dt = the average price change over the last 10 steps [t - 10 dt, t] [S].
  In the code, (dp/dt)/p is (p_t - p_(t-10dt)) / (0.1 p_(t-10dt)): divided by the price
  at the start of the window, not the current one (they differ by the price's move over
  the window, usually well under 1%; [S] does not say which). At the start the window
  is filled with the starting price, so the trend is 0 for the first 0.1 day.
- Order within a step: traders switch (secs. 1-2, all from the same state), then the
  price ticks (sec. 3), then the news moves the value (sec. 4) by Normal(0, sigma_eps sqrt(dt)).
- Floors: n_c and n_f never fall below a minimum, so neither group can die out for
  good (an "absorbing state") [S]. The value, 4 traders, is this project's choice:
  [S] and [C] give no number. When a step's moves would push a group below the floor,
  just enough of the moves out of that group are undone (the larger outflow first).
- Returns are measured once per unit of time: ret_t = ln p_t - ln p_(t-1) [N Fig 1].

## Runaways (not in the sources)
With some settings the price leaves its value for good: almost all traders become
chartists and the bubble never ends (parameter set I does this after about 28,500
days). The paper says this does not happen ("no persistent deviations"), so:
- a **runaway** = the price more than e (2.7x) away from its value for 250 trading
  days in a row, or ever more than e^20 away. The run stops with RunawayError.
- A bubble that goes past 2.7x and **bursts on its own** is not a runaway; it is
  the paper's mechanism, and it is kept.
- The S&P fit is stricter: the S&P 500 never sat 2.7x from any sensible value, so
  any such day disqualifies a setting.

## Fitting (herding/calibrate.py)
Random search over wide ranges, then Nelder-Mead from the best candidates. Every
candidate is scored on the same training seeds (100-107; the paper fit's search and
first refinement use only 100-101, because its runs are long, and `--refine` uses all 8);
every check uses other seeds (1000-1039).
- Paper fit: squared gaps to alpha 2.64 +/- 0.15, H 0.48 +/- 0.03, H|r| 0.85 +/- 0.03,
  plus a penalty if 25-day kurtosis is above 1. Runs of 50,000 days.
  These +/- values are the project's chosen yardsticks, not [N]'s error bars
  (alpha +/- 0.077, H +/- 0.003, H|r| +/- 0.010, Figs 2-3 captions). Those are

"""Drawing helpers shared by main.py, make_figures.py and (later) the web app.

One palette everywhere, checked for colour-blind safety (the dataviz validator:
blue, orange and aqua pass as a set of three in light mode):
    real market data         INK (near-black)
    S&P-calibrated model     BLUE
    paper-matched model      ORANGE
    no chartists / news      AQUA
Aqua is low-contrast on white, so it is always labelled (legend or text), never
identified by colour alone.
"""
from math import erfc
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from . import stats

INK, SECOND, MUTED, GRID = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9"
BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a"
BLUE_LIGHT, ORANGE_LIGHT = "#b7d3f6", "#f7c4ae"
REAL, SPX_MODEL, PAPER_MODEL, NEWS = INK, BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA

STYLE = {
    "figure.facecolor": "white", "axes.facecolor": "white",
    "axes.edgecolor": MUTED, "axes.labelcolor": SECOND, "axes.titlecolor": INK,
    "axes.titlesize": 10.5, "axes.labelsize": 9.5, "axes.titleweight": "bold",
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID, "grid.linewidth": 0.6,
    "xtick.color": SECOND, "ytick.color": SECOND, "xtick.labelsize": 8.5, "ytick.labelsize": 8.5,
    "legend.fontsize": 8.5, "legend.frameon": False, "lines.linewidth": 1.6,
    "font.family": "DejaVu Sans",
}


def style():
    plt.rcParams.update(STYLE)


def save(fig, path, title, caption):
    """Title on top, a plain-language caption underneath, save, close."""
    path = Path(path)
    fig.suptitle(title, x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=12.5, fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    fig.text(0.01, 0.005, caption, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=8.6, color=SECOND, wrap=True)
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    try:
        fig.savefig(path, dpi=130, bbox_inches="tight")
    finally:
        plt.close(fig)
    return path


def ccdf(ax, r, label, color, **kw):
    """Log-log tail plot: share of days whose |standardized return| exceeds x."""
    z, cc = stats.ccdf(r)
    keep = z > 0
    ax.loglog(z[keep], cc[keep], color=color, label=label, **kw)


def gaussian_ccdf(ax, label="bell curve N(0,1)"):
    g = np.geomspace(0.05, 6, 200)
    # share of a bell curve beyond +-x: erfc(x / sqrt 2). (math.erfc, not scipy: scipy
    # takes about half a second to load, in every worker process)
    ax.loglog(g, [erfc(x / np.sqrt(2)) for x in g], "--", color=MUTED, lw=1.2, label=label)


def dfa(ax, x, scales, label, color, marker="o", shift=1.0):
    """DFA fluctuation F(n) vs window n (log-log), with the fitted slope H in the label."""
    s, F = stats.dfa(x, scales)
    H = np.polyfit(np.log(s), np.log(F), 1)[0]
    ax.loglog(s, F * shift, marker, color=color, ms=4.5, lw=0,
              label=f"{label}: H = {H:.2f}")
    fit = np.exp(np.polyval(np.polyfit(np.log(s), np.log(F), 1), np.log(s)))
    ax.loglog(s, fit * shift, "-", color=color, lw=1.0)
    return H


def standardized(r):
    r = np.asarray(r, dtype=float)
    return (r - r.mean()) / r.std()


def comparison(real, model_r, z, no_chartists, path):
    """main.py's quick 2x2 overview: S&P vs model returns, tails, chartist share."""
    style()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7.5))
    n = min(len(real), len(model_r))
    for a, r, c, name in [(ax[0, 0], real[-n:], REAL, "S&P 500"),
                          (ax[0, 1], model_r[-n:], SPX_MODEL, "model (S&P-calibrated)")]:
        a.plot(standardized(r), lw=0.35, color=c)
        a.set_ylim(-25, 25)
        a.set_title(f"{name}: daily returns ({n:,} days)")
        a.set_ylabel("return / standard deviation")
    a = ax[1, 0]
    ccdf(a, real, "S&P 500", REAL)
    ccdf(a, model_r, "model", SPX_MODEL)
    ccdf(a, no_chartists, "model, no chartists", NEWS)
    gaussian_ccdf(a)
    a.set_xlim(0.3, 30)
    a.set_ylim(1e-5, 1.2)
    a.set_xlabel("|return| / standard deviation")
    a.set_ylabel("share of days with a bigger move")
    a.set_title("Tails: fat for the S&P and the model, thin without chartists")
    a.legend(loc="lower left")
    a = ax[1, 1]
    a.fill_between(np.arange(len(z)), 0, z, color=SPX_MODEL, lw=0)
    a.set_ylim(0, 1)
    a.set_title("Share of traders who are chartists (model)")
    a.set_xlabel("day")
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.04, 1, 0.95))
    return save(fig, path, "S&P 500 vs the herding model",
                "Model settings fitted to the S&P 500 (settings/spx.json); one held-out history shown.")
